issues.legal_issue: The Board’s general superintendence and control over subordinate revenue courts includes judicial as well as administrative power to correct illegal acts by those courts.
material_facts: The ceiling proceedings were governed by the earlier ceiling law, as the Board had directed in an earlier order.
The subordinate revenue officer determined the ceiling area under a later law despite that direction.
The Board found that the earlier law did not provide for separate units for the father and son.
issues.conclusion: The Board’s superintendence and control under Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, includes judicial power to intervene when a subordinate revenue court disregards the law or acts illegally.
issues.legal_principle: Section 221 is not made subject to the other provisions of the Act and confers both administrative and judicial superintendence over revenue courts. The Board may keep subordinate courts within their jurisdiction and correct an illegal act. The Court approved Kana v. Board of Revenue, ILR (1955) 5 Raj. 55; distinguished Karan Singh v. Board of Revenue, Rajasthan, 1962 Raj LW 178; and referred to Parmessar Singh v. Kailaspati, AIR 1916 Pat. 292 (FB), and the distinction between Sections 107 and 224(2) of the Government of India Acts of 1915 and 1935.

predicates.revenue_court_superintendence_case: The proceeding concerns the exercise of a supervisory power over a subordinate revenue court.
predicates.subordinate_court_acted_illegally: A subordinate revenue court disregarded a governing legal requirement or acted outside its lawful sphere.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns supervision of a subordinate revenue court and that court acted illegally, the Board has judicial supervisory power to correct the illegal act.

issues.legal_issue: The Board may set aside a subordinate revenue court’s order during a revision brought by another party, notwithstanding the State’s failure to appeal, when intervention is required in the interests of justice.
material_facts: The State did not appeal the subordinate officer’s order, which had allowed the father and son to be treated as separate units.
The father brought a revision challenging the determination of the land in his possession.
In that revision, the Board found that the subordinate officer had applied the later ceiling law despite an earlier direction to apply the earlier law.
The Board found that the earlier law did not provide for separate units and remanded the matter for fresh determination.
The Supreme Court held that the subordinate officer had committed a grave illegality by disregarding both the governing law and the Board’s direction.
issues.conclusion: The State’s failure to appeal did not prevent the Board from setting aside the subordinate orders and remanding the matter when the Board considered that the interests of justice required intervention.
issues.legal_principle: Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, contains no restriction preventing the Board from setting aside a subordinate court’s order when the interests of justice require it. Kana v. Board of Revenue, ILR (1955) 5 Raj. 55, recognized that supervisory power may be exercised sparingly in extraordinary cases where justice requires it. The Court also relied on the absence in Section 221 of a restriction like Section 224(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935.

rule.if: revenue_revision_proceeding and state_did_not_appeal and subordinate_court_ignored_prior_direction and subordinate_court_used_inapplicable_law and justice_requires_intervention

predicates.revenue_revision_proceeding: A party has brought a revision concerning an order made in a revenue proceeding.
predicates.state_did_not_appeal: The State did not appeal the subordinate court’s order.
predicates.subordinate_court_ignored_prior_directio: The subordinate court disregarded an earlier direction governing how it should decide the matter.
predicates.subordinate_court_used_inapplicable_law: The subordinate court decided the matter under a law that did not govern it.
predicates.justice_requires_intervention: The Board considered intervention necessary in the interests of justice.

issues.definition: In a revenue revision, if the State did not appeal but the subordinate court disregarded an earlier direction and used inapplicable law, the Board may set aside and remand the order when it considers intervention necessary in the interests of justice.
